title: Letters from the Mountain
author: Tadoku Note (original)
summary: 元郵便配達員の祖父と山で過ごす夏。手紙を運ばなくなった今も、祖父は山の家々を訪ね続けています。

source.note: Original text written for this app.

paragraphs: When Hana was twelve, her parents sent her to spend the summer with her grandfather, who lived alone in a village high in the mountains. There was no internet in the village, and her phone could not find a signal. On the first evening, she sat on the wooden step outside the house and felt that the summer would never end.

Her grandfather was a quiet man. He had been a postman for forty years, walking the steep mountain roads to bring letters to people in the small villages. Now he was retired, but he still woke up at five every morning and went for a long walk.
“Come with me tomorrow,” he said on the second day. Hana did not want to, but there was nothing else to do.

They walked up a narrow path through the forest. The air was cool and smelled of pine trees. After an hour, they reached a small house with a red roof. An old woman came out and greeted them warmly. She and Hana’s grandfather talked about the weather, the vegetables in her garden, and her knees, which hurt when it rained. Before they left, she gave them a bag of cucumbers.

This happened again and again over the following weeks. Her grandfather visited people who lived alone in the mountains, people he had once brought letters to. He did not bring letters anymore, but he brought newspapers, medicine from the town, or simply his company. Everyone was happy to see him.
“Why do you still do this?” Hana asked one day. “You’re not a postman anymore.”

Her grandfather thought about it as they walked. “When I was a postman,” he said, “I thought my job was to carry letters. But after a few years, I understood something. The letters were not the important part. The important part was that someone came. For many of these people, I was the only person they saw all week.”

Hana did not say anything, but she began to look at the mountain differently. She learned the names of the people they visited. She learned which ones liked to talk and which ones preferred to sit quietly. She learned that Mr. Ota, who never smiled, always kept a box of candy for visiting children.
At the end of August, it was time for Hana to go home. On her last morning, Mr. Ota gave her an envelope. “Open it on the train,” he said.

On the train, she opened it. Inside was a short letter, written carefully in pencil. “Thank you for visiting an old man,” it said. “Your grandfather brought me letters for forty years. This summer, you brought me something better. Please come back.”
Hana read the letter many times as the mountains disappeared behind her. When she got home, she found a sheet of paper and a pen. She had not written a letter by hand for years, maybe never.
